newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma warns against fresh disturbances in capital.
newsitem.headline: Burma warns against fresh disturbances in capital.

text.p: The Burmese military government on Thursday warned that it would not tolerate major civil disturbances in the tense capital as the latest wave of student unrest was muted by tight security measures.

Official media published the warning by Lieutenant General Tin Oo, a senior member of the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC), in a speech on Wednesday to civil servants and the state-run Union Solidarity and Development Association.

"The Secretary Two stressed that the SLORC will not accept such disturbances as in 1988 to break out again," the media reported, adding that he also urged civil servants to be loyal to the government.

Thousands of students, mainly from two troubled city universities, last week launched anti-government street protests. The SLORC broke up the demonstrations, held more than 860 protestors briefly and then freed them.
The protests were the biggest in Rangoon since the student-led, pro-democracy uprisings of September 1988 that the military crushed, leaving thousands dead or in jail.

The students last week were protesting police brutality in handling a brawl in October. They also demanded they be allowed to set up student unions on campuses and appealed for the universities to be kept open despite the protests.
Witnesses and diplomats said tight security measures launched by the military government in Rangoon kept students from launching fresh street protests.
Witnesses saw several truckloads of soldiers and riot police deployed in central Rangoon on Thursday morning, especially at a public square in front of the city hall.
Small groups of students continued to stage brief protests overnight inside some campuses, including those in two medical schools campuses, they added.
Troops and police blocked roads near the closed Yangon University and the Yangon Institute of Technology.
The tense situation forced the Yangon City Development Committee to postpone indefinitely the Rangoon Mayor's International Marathon scheduled for Saturday.
Sporadic student rallies also occurred in recent days outside the capital. Witnesses said about 200 students protested in the eastern town of Pa-an and were forcibly dispersed by police.

On Wednesday, the government accused the United States of trying to use the SLORC's restrictions on opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi's movements during the student unrest as an excuse to impose sanctions on the country.
It also accused the American Embassy in Rangoon of encouraging Suu Kyi to come out while the SLORC had asked her to temporarily stay at home for her own safety.
An embassy official denied the accusation.
Suu Kyi's aides said she has since remained at her lakeside home to avoid being drawn into any unrest.
